title: Dandelion
subtitle: The common bitter: root decoctions and leaf infusions for digestion and fluid balance
excerpt: Dandelion is the garden weed whose root and leaves are the most accessible bitter digestive herbs in western herbal practice. The dried root is decocted for a bitter liver and digestive tonic; the leaves make a mild diuretic infusion. Both root and leaf keep 12 months dried in a sealed tin.

glossaryTerms.definition: A herb containing bitter compounds that, when tasted before or during a meal, stimulate the secretion of digestive juices, traditionally used to support appetite and digestion.
A herb traditionally used to increase urine output and reduce mild fluid retention, often used for short periods to relieve bloating.

attrs.body: Not medical advice. Consult a qualified herbalist or doctor before use. Full precautions are in the 'When not to use' section.

content.text: Taraxacum officinale Weber ex F.H.Wigg., family Asteraceae. A rosette-forming perennial, familiar across lawns, road verges, and disturbed ground throughout the temperate world. The root is long, tapering, white inside, brown outside, harvested in autumn when the root has stored the bitter sesquiterpene lactones that give it its digestive action. The leaves, the dandelion clock rosette, are harvested in spring when youngest. Both dry well at home.

The root carries bitter compounds, inulin (a plant sugar, highest in autumn root), and triterpenes. These give dandelion its bitter digestive action and the traditional use for liver and gallbladder support. The leaf carries potassium (high enough to compensate for its diuretic effect), vitamins A and C, and plant pigments. Current herbal guidance supports the root for digestive complaints and loss of appetite, and the leaf for mild fluid retention.

The 17th-century herbalist Culpeper recommended dandelion for the liver, gallbladder, and spleen. The 20th-century herbalist Grieve covers root herbal brews for liver support and as a spring tonic. The Eclectic tradition used dandelion root as a digestive bitter and bile-stimulating herb. Current herbal guidance supports traditional use for root in digestive complaints and for leaf as a mild diuretic.

Root herbal brew: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried root per 200 ml of cold water. Bring to a simmer, cover, and simmer for 15 to 20 minutes. Strain and drink half a cup before meals, up to twice a day. The taste is bitter and earthy. honey does not improve it significantly but a little lemon helps.

Leaf infusion: 1 to 2 teaspoons of dried dandelion leaf (or a generous handful of fresh young leaves) per 200 ml of just-boiled water, steeped covered for 8 minutes. One to two cups a day. A mild diuretic best taken in the morning rather than at bedtime.

Prescribed diuretics: the leaf has a documented diuretic effect. Taking it alongside furosemide, thiazides, or other prescribed diuretics may increase the diuretic effect more than intended. Discuss with your prescriber.
Kidney stones: dandelion leaf is high in oxalate. Anyone with a history of calcium oxalate stones should avoid regular use.

Gallstones: dandelion root stimulates bile production and bile flow. Where gallstones are present, this stimulation can trigger biliary colic. Consult a herbalist or doctor before using dandelion root if you have known gallstones.
